video_title: Amanda Lynam, Chief Credit Strategist in Global Investment Research, Goldman Sachs
gist: Goldman Sachs credit strategist Amanda Lynam argues corporate credit spreads are technically, not fundamentally, driven right now, with a multi-trillion-dollar AI/hyperscaler debt issuance wave (only 40% of which is hyperscalers themselves) pushing investors to redefine 'quality' as moving down in ratings rather than up, while foreign demand and yield-based buying provide a resilient but potentially fragile floor under spreads.

themes.theme: AI capex and the hyperscaler debt supply wave

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs equity research estimates hyperscaler capex from 2026 through 2030 at more than $6 trillion (even larger once 2031 and already-invested 2025 capital are included), but hyperscalers account for only 40% of total AI-related gross debt issuance, meaning the credit exposure to the AI theme is much broader than the mega-cap names alone.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Investors who screen AI credit risk by looking only at hyperscaler bonds are missing roughly 60% of the actual AI-related debt universe; broader issuer screens are needed.
insights.quote: what we found in our work is that actually the hyperscalers are only 40% of total AI related gross issuance. So the theme is actually much broader.

insights.claim: Hyperscalers issued $108 billion of global investment-grade debt in 2025, already $229 billion by mid-September 2026, with Goldman forecasting $250 billion for full-year 2026 and a 60% jump to $400 billion in 2027, plus an additional roughly $300 billion of data-center and chip project financing in 2027 that is separate from direct hyperscaler debt.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete supply calendar (accelerating through 2027) that credit investors can use to time new-issue concessions and spread-widening risk.
insights.quote: we're penciling in 400 billion of global hyperscaler direct debt issuance and again here I'm just thinking about the debt issuance from the hyperscalers ... that's another 300 billion for those keeping track in 2027

insights.claim: Goldman models the debt-financed share of hyperscaler capex peaking at 35% in 2027, reflecting a lag of three months to two years between AI investment and monetization, but expects absolute issuance to keep growing in later years even after that ratio peaks because total capex remains abundant.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Issuance won't necessarily taper once the debt-financed percentage peaks in 2027 — absolute dollar supply can keep climbing, arguing against a near-term relief in primary market pressure.

insights.claim: Goldman raised its 2026 US investment-grade gross issuance forecast to $2.3 trillion (from $2.1 trillion) and is penciling in $2.4 trillion for 2027, which would set a nominal record above the pandemic-era issuance boom (not inflation-adjusted), showing the hyperscaler wave is arriving inside an already record-setting broader capital markets cycle.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Context for crowding-out fears: the denominator (total IG supply) is expanding alongside hyperscaler issuance, somewhat diluting single-theme concentration risk while confirming a structurally larger primary calendar to absorb.
insights.quote: for 2027, we're actually penciling in 2.4 trillion of overall US IG gross issuance.

insights.claim: AI-related debt broadly defined is about 12% of the US investment-grade bond index by notional, versus the tech sector alone at roughly 10%, but it still trails the global banking sector at about 21-22% of the index, so AI is meaningful but not yet the largest single sector risk in IG.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Counters the narrative that AI issuance already dominates IG credit indices; banks remain the largest sector concentration, a useful anchor for sector risk models.

insights.claim: A large share of AI-related financing — data center and chip project finance — is done through private 144A-for-life placements or double-B-rated high-yield project bonds that are not index-eligible in IG, so standard bond-index composition understates true AI-related credit exposure in the market.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Analysts relying purely on public index sector weights will underestimate real AI-related credit exposure across the market; private and project-finance channels need to be tracked separately.

themes.theme: Credit backdrop: constructive but technically driven

insights.claim: Goldman is generally constructive on corporate credit due to at-or-above-trend growth, solid leverage and coverage fundamentals, and a powerful technical bid from yield-based investors (insurers, pensions, foreign buyers), but still forecasts modest spread widening because current tightness is hard to sustain against record issuance.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Base case is a slow grind toward wider spreads, not a directional short signal — periods of widening have historically been short-lived and hard to trade around.

insights.claim: The key risk to the constructive credit view is a tipping point where rising rates volatility flips the rates market from a tailwind into a headwind for credit spreads; what matters is not a specific yield level but what is driving the yield backup — resilient growth is digestible for credit, while a fiscal-driven backup is not.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Watch rates volatility and the narrative behind Treasury yield moves (growth-driven vs. fiscal-driven) as the key regime-change signal for credit spreads, rather than any fixed yield threshold.
insights.quote: It's incredibly difficult to time that... I really push back on pinpointing of value because I think it's far more about what are the drivers of the backup in yields and what is the velocity of that.

insights.claim: Only about 15-20% of the all-in yield in US and European investment-grade credit currently comes from the credit spread itself, with the rest from the risk-free rate, versus a much larger spread contribution during 2010-2021, meaning IG now behaves much more like a rates product than a pure credit product.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Rates/duration risk management now matters more than idiosyncratic spread selection for IG total returns; Treasury moves will dominate IG performance more than credit-specific factors.

insights.claim: Goldman believes leveraged finance is already past peak defaults for this cycle, since distressed exchanges and formal defaults have largely already worked through the market, leaving current stress concentrated and lagging rather than signaling a fresh wave of deterioration.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Argues against a fresh 'credit cycle turn' narrative; investors betting on rising default rates from here may be fighting a cycle that already peaked.
insights.quote: we actually think we're past peak defaults for this cycle

insights.claim: The riskiest pocket for interest-coverage deterioration is the credit market's 'left tail' — triple-C rated US and European high yield, and small private-credit borrowers from vintages formed in ultra-low-rate environments — where interest coverage is near or below 1x for some names, while broad IG and high-yield fundamentals remain solid.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Credit stress should stay idiosyncratic and concentrated in CCC and small private-credit names rather than broad-based, useful for targeted shorts/avoidance rather than broad market hedges.

insights.claim: Historically moving up in ratings (AA in IG, BB in high yield) signaled a defensive posture, but today that means buying into the ratings tiers most saturated with AI-related supply and carrying more duration with a thinner spread cushion, so Goldman now sees moving down in quality — overweight BBBs versus higher-rated IG, and overweight single-Bs versus BBs in high yield — as the more defensive relative-value trade.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Actionable relative-value tilt: overweight BBB in IG and single-B in high yield versus higher-rated tranches, on the view that AI supply and duration risk are concentrated at the top of the ratings spectrum.
insights.quote: the more attractive relative value posturing that we see is to selectively move down in credit quality.

insights.claim: Goldman is selectively overweight the triple-C cohort within high yield despite calling it the market's left tail, implying the opportunity there is name-specific security selection rather than a blanket sector allocation.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Signals opportunity in CCC credit is bottom-up and idiosyncratic, relevant for distressed and special-situations investors rather than broad beta positioning.

themes.theme: Foreign demand, rates, and the crowding-out debate

insights.claim: Federal Reserve data shows 29% of the US corporate bond market is owned by foreign investors (likely understated due to flows routed through domestic asset managers), and foreign investors bought a net $251 billion of US corporate credit in the first half of 2026 alone, putting 2026 on pace to exceed 2025's full-year record.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: The foreign bid remains a structural pillar under US credit spreads; a slowdown here (from FX hedging costs or currency dynamics) is a key spread-widening trigger to monitor.
insights.quote: foreign investors purchased 251 billion on net of US corporate credit, which puts 2026 on pace to exceed the fullyear record which was set in 2025.

insights.claim: More than half of foreign inflows into US credit come from Europe, not Japan, even though market commentary around Scott Bessent and yen intervention has focused on Japanese repatriation risk; a Bank of Japan financial stability report from April 2026 actually shows Japanese banks rotating toward CLOs, alternatives and private equity and away from IG and high-yield corporate bonds — a marginal negative for that cohort, not the dominant flow.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: The popular 'Japan repatriation' risk narrative to US credit is overstated relative to actual flow data; European demand is the more important swing factor to track for US credit spreads.

insights.claim: Goldman sees very little evidence that hyperscaler debt issuance is crowding out other borrowers or driving Treasury yields higher; its rates strategists attribute recent upward Treasury yield momentum more to commodity market moves, and any rates-market pressure from heavy IG issuance is mechanical (dealers/investors hedging new-issue interest rate risk by shorting Treasuries), not an asset-allocation crowding-out effect.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Pushes back on a popular bear thesis that AI capex is crowding out government or industrial borrowers; investors should not overweight this fear in rates or credit models currently.
insights.quote: we actually see very little evidence of a crowding out as it relates to the hyperscaler issuance.

themes.theme: High yield and private credit market structure

insights.claim: Barriers to entry into the syndicated high-yield bond market have risen sharply: the average new-issue size in US high yield is about $900 million in 2026 (versus a few hundred million in prior years) and above $1.5 billion in investment grade, pushing smaller and earlier-stage borrowers toward private credit instead — the real driver behind high yield's migration up in quality and its unusually muted spread/index volatility.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Explains why HY cash indices (e.g., HYG) trade so quietly structurally, relevant for options and volatility traders in that space, and reframes private credit growth as a market-structure shift rather than purely a story of risky borrowers fleeing.
insights.quote: the average new issue size in USIG was comfortably above 1.5 billion so far this year. And the average new issue size in the high yield bond market has been around 900 million in 2026

insights.claim: Goldman pushes back on the narrative that private credit mainly absorbs 'more vulnerable' issuers fleeing public high yield, arguing instead that it primarily serves smaller issuers who need bespoke, incremental financing earlier in their growth journey.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Tempers the common bear thesis that private credit is a hidden risk-dumping ground; helps investors calibrate how much systemic weight to put on private credit growth headlines.

insights.claim: Goldman is not concerned about a broad near-term maturity wall (IG has been steadily refinancing low-rate debt for years), but flags the 2028-2029 software maturity wall in leveraged loans and private credit as a genuine watch item given the unresolved risk of AI disrupting legacy software business models.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete forward catalyst window (2028-2029) for credit stress specifically in software-sector loans and private credit, distinct from the broader, largely benign refinancing picture.

themes.theme: Portfolio construction and hidden AI exposure

insights.claim: A recent Federal Reserve rate hike has pushed base rates higher again, which will likely stall the recent modest improvement seen in floating-rate borrowers' interest coverage as they refinance into elevated benchmark rates.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Monitor floating-rate loan and private-credit coverage metrics for renewed deterioration given the higher-for-longer rate path implied by the recent hike.

insights.claim: AI factor exposure can hide inside allocations that don't look AI-related on the surface — such as utilities selling power to data centers or EM/South Korea exposure via memory chipmakers — so Goldman discounts these 'AI-tangential' sectors, assuming only about 30% of issuance from sectors like utilities and machinery is truly AI-related when building its AI-exposure screen.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Investors building 'ex-AI' diversified books should stress-test utilities, EM, and industrials allocations for embedded AI/data-center beta, not just tech and hyperscaler bonds directly.

insights.claim: Amid the AI issuance wave, credit allocators are placing extra diversification value on healthcare/pharma, food and beverage, energy and banks specifically because they are non-AI sectors, with energy additionally well-bid as a geopolitical hedge and pharma/healthcare carrying some optionality on AI-driven drug-discovery upside.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: These sectors could see structurally tighter spreads or relative outperformance purely from diversification demand as AI-related supply keeps growing, independent of their own fundamentals.

insights.claim: Goldman's portfolio strategy team sees a broader post-financial-crisis shift away from the traditional 60/40 portfolio toward including more real assets — commodities, infrastructure, real estate — for inflation pass-through and diversification, sometimes framed as a '50/30/20' allocation, a trend viewed as durable independent of the AI cycle.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: A structural allocation shift worth tracking or replicating in portfolio construction beyond credit, and a tailwind for growth of infrastructure/real-asset debt issuance.

insights.claim: By 2028 and beyond, Goldman expects the binding constraint on hyperscaler financing to be market conventions around single-issuer and single-theme concentration limits, not the hyperscalers' ability to raise debt while staying investment-grade, implying private markets will have to absorb a growing share of the AI financing load as public IG capacity for any one theme gets saturated.
insights.speaker: Amanda Lynam
insights.so_what: Sets up private credit and private placements as likely 2028-plus beneficiaries of the AI capex cycle, and flags issuer-concentration limits — not credit quality — as the real ceiling on public hyperscaler bond issuance.
